Mechanism_Q: How does the cirrhotic nodule-to-HCC pathway explain the shift toward arterial-phase hyperenhancement?
Mechanism: Core describes progression in cirrhosis from regenerative nodule -> dysplastic nodule -> HCC. Regenerative nodules are portal-vein supplied and should not arterially enhance; most dysplastic nodules also remain predominantly portal supplied, although high-grade dysplastic nodules can begin to enhance arterially. HCC develops neovascularity and the classic phenotype becomes arterial hyperenhancement with portal venous/delayed washout and capsule. Radiology pivot: increasing arterialization within the cirrhotic nodule pathway moves the lesion toward HCC, while regenerative/low-grade dysplastic nodules usually lack the full pattern.

Mechanism_Q: Why does hepatic adenoma usually show little HIDA uptake and often appear photopenic on sulfur-colloid scintigraphy?
Mechanism: Core describes hepatic adenoma as hepatocytes with scattered Kupffer cells but no bile ducts. The absence of biliary ductules explains the paucity of HIDA uptake. Sulfur-colloid uptake depends on reticuloendothelial/Kupffer-cell activity, so adenomas are usually photopenic, although Core notes this is not absolute. Radiology pivot: FNH contains bile ductules and more functional Kupffer-cell architecture, so HIDA/sulfur-colloid behavior can help separate FNH from adenoma.

High_Yield_Q: On CT, what imaging findings define the AAST liver injury grades I-V in Core Radiology?
High_Yield_A:
Grade I: subcapsular hematoma <10% surface or laceration <1 cm.
Grade II: subcapsular hematoma 10-50%, intraparenchymal hematoma <10 cm, or laceration 1-3 cm.
Grade III: subcapsular hematoma >50%, ruptured hematoma, laceration >3 cm, or contained vascular injury/active bleeding.
Grade IV: laceration involving 25-75% of one lobe or active bleeding extending into the peritoneum.
Grade V: >75% lobar destruction or retrohepatic IVC/central hepatic vein injury.
Exam pivot: Grade the highest imaging injury; multiple injuries advance one grade up to grade III.

Recognition pivot: Hypervascularity plus hemorrhagic/fat heterogeneity supports adenoma but overlaps HCC.

High_Yield_Q: When a hemorrhagic hepatic mass is hypervascular, what source-supported clues favor adenoma versus HCC?
High_Yield_A:

HCC: intratumoral spontaneous hemorrhage is uncommon, but large HCC may rupture; cirrhotic background, arterial hypervascularity with washout, and capsule favor HCC.
Key differentiator: Use patient substrate plus the full multiphasic pattern, not hemorrhage alone.
